description: Mind-blowing daily technical trivia and computer facts for YouTube Shorts

facts.title: The First Computer Bug Was a Real Moth
facts.hook: Did you know why software errors are called bugs?
facts.script: Did you know why computer errors are called 'bugs'? In 1947, computer pioneer Grace Hopper was working on the Harvard Mark Two computer when it stopped working. When engineers opened the machine, they found an actual dead moth trapped inside a relay switch! Hopper taped the moth into the logbook, officially naming it the 'First actual case of bug being found'. Subscribe for more crazy tech facts!

facts.title: The First 1GB Hard Drive Weighed 500 Pounds
facts.hook: How heavy was the world's first 1 Gigabyte hard drive?
facts.script: Imagine carrying a 1 Gigabyte flash drive that weighs as much as a refrigerator! In 1980, IBM released the IBM 3380—the world's first commercial hard drive with 1 Gigabyte of storage. It weighed over 550 pounds and cost forty thousand dollars! Today, a tiny microSD card the size of your fingernail holds a thousand times more data for just ten dollars. Follow for more tech evolution facts!

facts.title: Why is QWERTY the Keyboard Standard?
facts.hook: Why are keyboard keys not in alphabetical order?
facts.script: Ever wondered why your keyboard isn't ABCDEF? The QWERTY layout was invented in 1873 by Christopher Sholes for mechanical typewriters. When typists typed too fast on alphabetical layouts, the metal type bars would collide and jam! Sholes placed frequently used letter pairs farther apart to slow typists down slightly and prevent mechanical jams. Even in the digital age, we still use this 150-year-old anti-jamming layout!

facts.title: Why 404 Means Page Not Found
facts.hook: Where did the famous Error 404 come from?
facts.script: Why does '404' mean Page Not Found? When Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web at CERN in Switzerland, HTTP status codes were created with a simple logic: 4xx codes mean Client-Side Errors, and 04 specifically indicates 'Object Not Found'. Urban legend says Room 404 at CERN housed the original central database, but in reality, it's just pure elegant network protocol engineering!

facts.title: Your Smartphone Has More Power Than Apollo 11
facts.hook: How powerful is your phone compared to NASA moon missions?
facts.script: The Apollo Guidance Computer that took Neil Armstrong to the Moon in 1969 had just 4 Kilobytes of RAM and ran at 0.043 Megahertz. Today, the smartphone in your pocket has over millions of times more processing power and storage than the entire NASA command center that put humanity on the Moon! You are holding a supercomputer in your hands!

facts.title: Why Python is Named After a Comedy Show
facts.hook: Is Python named after the snake?
facts.script: Most people think Python was named after the dangerous snake, but that's completely false! In 1989, creator Guido van Rossum was looking for a short, unique, and slightly mysterious name while reading published scripts from 'Monty Python's Flying Circus'—a famous BBC comedy series. Guido was a huge fan of the comedy group, so he named the language Python! Subscribe for more coding trivia!

facts.title: 90 Percent of World Currency is Just Digital Numbers
facts.hook: How much physical cash actually exists in the world?
facts.script: Did you know that only about 8 to 10 percent of the world's money exists as physical coins and banknotes? The remaining 90 percent exists purely as digital bits and bytes stored in bank database servers and ledger algorithms. When you swipe a card or transfer money, no physical money moves—computers just update numeric records in milliseconds!

facts.title: The First Computer Mouse Was Made of Wood
facts.hook: What was the very first computer mouse made of?
facts.script: In 1964, Douglas Engelbart invented the world's very first computer mouse at Stanford Research Institute. It wasn't made of sleek plastic or aluminum—it was carved out of a block of pine wood with two metal wheels underneath to track movement! It was called a 'mouse' because the electrical cord came out of the back resembling a tail. Follow for more tech origins!

facts.title: There are Over 700 Programming Languages
facts.hook: How many coding languages exist in the world?
facts.script: While most developers only know Python, JavaScript, C++, and Java, computer scientists have created over 700 distinct programming languages! Some were created as jokes, like 'Brainfuck' and 'Cow', while others like Fortran and COBOL still process over 70 percent of global ATM transactions today. Subscribe for daily tech insights!

facts.title: Undersea Cables Carry 99 Percent of Global Internet
facts.hook: Does satellite or undersea cable power international internet?
facts.script: Many people assume international internet runs through space satellites, but in reality, over 99 percent of international data travels through fiber optic cables lying on the bottom of the ocean floor! There are over 500 undersea submarine cables stretching over 1.4 million kilometers—enough to circle the Earth 35 times! Follow for more internet secrets!

facts.title: The First Website Ever is Still Online
facts.hook: Did you know the world's very first website created in 1991 is still online today?
facts.script: The world's first website was published on August 6, 1991, by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. It was dedicated to information about the World Wide Web project. You can still visit the original page today at info.cern.ch!

facts.title: Email Existed Before the Internet
facts.hook: Did you know that email was invented before the internet even existed?
facts.script: In 1965, the MAILBOX system at MIT allowed users on the same mainframe computer to leave messages for each other. It wasn't until 1971 that Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email using the @ symbol on ARPANET!

facts.title: A Single Google Search Takes Less Energy Than a Heartbeat
facts.hook: Ever wondered how much computing power happens during a single Google search?
facts.script: A single Google query uses approximately 0.0003 kilowatt-hours of energy and consults over 1,000 servers in less than 0.2 seconds. That computation takes less energy than the human body consumes in a single heartbeat!

facts.title: CAPTCHA Digitized Millions of Books
facts.hook: Did you know those annoying 'I am not a robot' tests helped transcribe millions of ancient books?
facts.script: When you solved reCAPTCHA words in the late 2000s, one word was for verification, while the second was an unreadable scanned word from the Google Books archive. Millions of humans collectively digitized entire historical libraries!

facts.title: The First Computer Programmer Was a Woman in 1843
facts.hook: Who was the world's first computer programmer?
facts.script: Ada Lovelace wrote the world's first machine algorithm in 1843 for Charles Babbage's mechanical Analytical Engine. She realized computers could manipulate not just numbers, but anything representable by symbols, including music and art!

facts.title: The First Domain Name Ever Registered
facts.hook: What was the very first .com domain name in history?
facts.script: On March 15, 1985, Symbolics.com became the first registered .com domain name in history, registered by the Symbolics Computer Corporation. Today, over 370 million domain names exist worldwide!

facts.title: Your GPU Calculates Millions of Triangles Every Second
facts.hook: How do modern graphics cards render photorealistic 3D worlds?
facts.script: Modern GPUs contain thousands of micro-cores working simultaneously. To draw a 3D game character or environment, the GPU calculates the lighting, texture, and geometry of over 50 million polygons and triangles every single second!

facts.title: WiFi Doesn't Stand for Wireless Fidelity
facts.hook: Did you know WiFi does not stand for Wireless Fidelity?
facts.script: The term 'WiFi' was actually created in 1999 by branding firm Interbrand as a catchy consumer-friendly name for the IEEE 802.11b wireless networking standard. It was never an acronym for Wireless Fidelity!

facts.title: The Password for US Nuclear Missiles Was 00000000
facts.hook: What was the most insecure critical computer password in history?
facts.script: For nearly 20 years during the Cold War, the launch code for US Minuteman nuclear missiles was set to eight zeros: 00000000. It was chosen to ensure missiles could be launched instantly without delay during an emergency!

facts.title: Linux Runs 100 Percent of the Top 500 Supercomputers
facts.hook: Which operating system controls the most powerful machines on Earth?
facts.script: Every single one of the world's Top 500 fastest supercomputers runs on Linux. From weather forecasting and nuclear simulations to large-scale AI training, open-source Linux dominates high-performance supercomputing!

facts.title: The First Digital Camera Weighed 8 Pounds
facts.hook: How big was the very first digital camera?
facts.script: In 1975, Kodak engineer Steve Sasson invented the first digital camera. It weighed 8 pounds, captured black-and-white 0.01 megapixel photos, and took 23 seconds to record the image onto a standard cassette tape!

facts.title: Why Computer Memory is Counted in Powers of 2
facts.hook: Why do phones and computers come in 64GB, 128GB, or 256GB?
facts.script: Because computers operate in binary (base-2), memory chips are addressed using electrical binary lines. Adding a single address line doubles the addressable memory capacity: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and 1024!

facts.title: The First Computer Mouse Was Made of Wood
facts.hook: Did you know Douglas Engelbart made the first computer mouse out of a wooden block?
facts.script: In 1964, Douglas Engelbart built the first prototype computer mouse using a carved wooden shell and two metal wheels. It was called a 'mouse' because the cord tail extending out the back resembled a real rodent!

facts.title: NASA Still Uses 1970s Technology on Voyager 1
facts.hook: How much memory does NASA's farthest spacecraft possess?
facts.script: Voyager 1, currently over 15 billion miles away in interstellar space, runs on three computers with just 69 kilobytes of memory combined. That is millions of times less memory than a modern smart lightbulb!

facts.title: Bluetooth Was Named After a Viking King
facts.hook: Did you know Bluetooth is named after a 10th-century Scandinavian King?
facts.script: Intel engineer Jim Kardach named the technology after King Harald Bluetooth, who united Scandinavian tribes. Just as the king united tribes, Bluetooth was designed to unite communication protocols across PC and cellular devices!

facts.title: Over 5 Billion Videos are Watched on YouTube Daily
facts.hook: How much video data flows across YouTube every single day?
facts.script: Every minute, over 500 hours of video are uploaded to YouTube. That equals over 720,000 hours of video per day! Google uses intelligent distributed storage clusters to encode and stream petabytes of video in real time!

facts.title: The First Video Game Was Created in 1958
facts.hook: What was the very first electronic video game?
facts.script: In October 1958, physicist William Higinbotham created 'Tennis for Two' using an analog computer and a 5-inch oscilloscope screen at Brookhaven National Laboratory. It was the world's first interactive electronic game!

facts.title: Why Transistors are Approaching the Size of Atoms
facts.hook: How small are the transistors inside your smartphone chip?
facts.script: Modern 3-nanometer microchips contain over 15 billion transistors packed into a chip the size of a fingernail. A single transistor is now only about 15 silicon atoms wide, reaching the limits of quantum physics!

facts.title: The First Computer Virus Was Created as a Prank in 1971
facts.hook: What did the world's very first computer virus do?
facts.script: In 1971, Bob Thomas created the 'Creeper virus' on ARPANET. It didn't damage files—it simply printed: 'I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!' It led to the creation of the first antivirus program called Reaper!

facts.title: Why 1 Kilobyte is 1024 Bytes Instead of 1000
facts.hook: Why isn't a kilobyte exactly 1,000 bytes?
facts.script: In decimal metric systems, 'kilo' means 1,000. But computers calculate in binary powers of 2. 2 to the power of 10 equals 1,024, which is the closest binary number to 1,000, creating the binary kilobyte standard!

facts.title: Why Every iPhone Ad Displays Exactly 9:41 AM
facts.hook: Have you ever noticed that every Apple iPhone commercial displays 9:41 AM on the clock?
facts.script: When Steve Jobs unveiled the very first iPhone in 2007, his keynote was timed so the slide appeared at approximately 9:42 AM. Apple later adjusted it to 9:41 AM, and to this day, every official Apple product launch photo is set to 9:41!

facts.title: Google Was Originally Named BackRub
facts.hook: Did you know that Google's original name was actually BackRub?
facts.script: In 1996, Larry Page and Sergey Brin named their revolutionary search engine BackRub because it analyzed web back-links to determine page importance. They renamed it Google in 1997, inspired by the mathematical term Googol, representing a 1 followed by 100 zeros!

facts.title: The First Webcam Was Created to Watch a Coffee Pot
facts.hook: Why did Cambridge University scientists invent the world's first webcam?
facts.script: In 1991, researchers in the Cambridge computer lab were tired of walking down three flights of stairs only to find the Trojan Room coffee pot empty! They pointed a video camera at the pot and streamed 1 frame per second to their computer screens, creating the world's first live webcam!

facts.title: Why Dark Mode Saves Up to 60 Percent Battery on OLED
facts.hook: Does dark mode really save phone battery, or is it just an aesthetic myth?
facts.script: On OLED and AMOLED smartphone screens, each individual sub-pixel produces its own light. When a pixel displays true black, that pixel turns off completely and consumes zero electrical power! Tests show dark mode can save up to 60% battery life on OLED displays!

facts.title: GPS Requires Einstein's Theory of Relativity to Work
facts.hook: Did you know GPS satellites would fail in minutes without Einstein's physics?
facts.script: Because GPS satellites orbit 12,000 miles above Earth moving at 8,700 miles per hour, gravitational time dilation makes their onboard atomic clocks tick 38 microseconds faster every day! Engineers must continuously apply Einstein's general and special relativity formulas, or your map would drift by 6 miles every single day!

facts.title: CAPTCHA Tests Were Secretly Training Self-Driving AI
facts.hook: Why do CAPTCHA security tests constantly ask you to click traffic lights and crosswalks?
facts.script: When Google acquired reCAPTCHA, they trained neural networks for Waymo self-driving cars! Every time hundreds of millions of internet users click stop signs, motorcycles, and fire hydrants to prove they are human, they are actually labeling high-difficulty edge cases for autonomous driving vision models!

facts.title: Why Transistors are Approaching the Size of Atoms
facts.hook: How small are the transistors inside your smartphone processor?
facts.script: Modern 3-nanometer computer chips pack over 15 billion transistors onto a silicon wafer the size of your fingernail! At this microscopic scale, the gate of a transistor is only about 10 to 15 silicon atoms wide, and electrons can literally quantum-tunnel straight through barriers!

facts.title: The Entire Internet Weights About 50 Grams of Electrons
facts.hook: How much does all the stored data on the entire internet weigh?
facts.script: Physicist John Kubiatowicz calculated that storing data on silicon flash memory trapped extra electrons. Storing an entire web server's petabytes of data adds an immeasurably tiny mass of moving electrical charge. In total, all the active electricity powering the global internet weighs approximately 50 grams—about the weight of a single strawberry!

facts.title: Why Ethernet Cables Have Twisted Pairs of Wires
facts.hook: Why are the colorful copper wires inside an internet cable tightly twisted together?
facts.script: In 1881, Alexander Graham Bell discovered that twisting pairs of telephone wires together balanced out electromagnetic interference! In modern Cat6 Ethernet cables, each twisted pair cancels out external radiation and cross-talk from neighboring wires, allowing gigabit signals to transmit without data corruption!

facts.title: The First Commercial Hard Drive Was Leased for $3,200 a Month
facts.hook: How much did the world's very first computer hard disk cost in 1956?
facts.script: The IBM 350 RAMAC disk storage unit arrived in 1956. It weighed over one ton, used fifty 24-inch magnetic platters, and stored just 3.75 megabytes of data! IBM refused to sell it outright and instead leased it to businesses for $3,200 per month—equivalent to over $36,000 per month today!

facts.title: Why Keyboard Keys Are Staggered Instead of Aligned
facts.hook: Why aren't computer keyboard keys arranged in a straight vertical grid?
facts.script: Modern keyboards inherit their layout from mechanical typewriters built in the 1870s! Each key was connected to a physical metal strike lever. If keys were aligned in straight columns, the mechanical levers would collide and jam constantly. The staggering prevented mechanical jams, and computers simply kept the tradition!

facts.title: Over 90 Percent of World Passwords Are in the RockYou Wordlist
facts.hook: What is the most famous password leak database in cybersecurity history?
facts.script: In 2009, a company called RockYou was breached, leaking over 32 million plaintext passwords stored without encryption! Security researchers compiled this into the legendary 'rockyou.txt' wordlist. Today, automated hacking bots use this exact list to crack millions of weak user passwords in milliseconds!

facts.title: Why Minecraft Worlds Are Limited by 64-Bit Integer Bounds
facts.hook: Why does Minecraft's infinite world glitch out at 30 million blocks?
facts.script: Minecraft calculates coordinates using 64-bit floating point numbers. As players travel past 30 million blocks from spawn, the mathematical precision of floating-point coordinates degrades, causing the physics engine and terrain generation to break down into the famous 'Far Lands' glitch!

facts.title: Why macOS and iOS Are Built on Top of UNIX
facts.hook: What operating system actually powers Apple's iPhones and Macs under the hood?
facts.script: When Steve Jobs returned to Apple with NeXT in 1997, he brought NeXTSTEP, an operating system built on the open-source BSD UNIX kernel called Darwin. Beneath Apple's sleek interface lies a genuine POSIX-certified UNIX foundation that powers macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS!

facts.title: The First Computer Bug Was Removed with Tweezers
facts.hook: Where did the phrase 'debugging a computer' literally come from?
facts.script: On September 9, 1947, computer pioneer Grace Hopper's team was troubleshooting the Harvard Mark II relay computer. Inside Relay 70, they discovered an actual moth stuck between the electrical contacts! They removed it with tweezers, taped it into their daily logbook, and wrote: 'First actual case of bug being found!'

facts.title: Why SSDs Wear Out Over Time While HDDs Don't Suffer Write Fatigue
facts.hook: Why do solid state drives have a finite write lifespan?
facts.script: NAND flash memory stores data by trapping electrons inside floating-gate transistors using high-voltage tunneling. Over time, each write and erase cycle physically degrades the microscopic silicon dioxide insulating layer until the cell can no longer hold charge reliably. Modern SSD controllers use wear-leveling algorithms to spread writes evenly across trillions of cells!

facts.title: The First Video Uploaded to YouTube Was Shot at a Zoo
facts.hook: What was the very first video ever uploaded to YouTube?
facts.script: On April 23, 2005, YouTube co-founder Jawed Karim uploaded a 19-second video titled 'Me at the zoo'. Standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo, he casually commented on their trunks. That single 19-second test clip launched the largest video sharing network in human history!

facts.title: Why Python Uses Indentation Instead of Curly Braces
facts.hook: Why is Python the only mainstream language that enforces whitespace indentation?
facts.script: Python creator Guido van Rossum hated how programmers wrote messy, unreadable code with mismatched curly braces in C and Java. He decided that since developers already indent their code for readability, the Python compiler should use indentation itself as the block structure, making Python the most readable language on Earth!

facts.title: Why 1 Byte Equals 8 Bits
facts.hook: Why did computer scientists standardize a byte to exactly 8 bits instead of 10?
facts.script: In the early computing era, character sets like IBM's EBCDIC and the 7-bit ASCII standard required an 8th bit for parity error-checking across memory buses. In 1964, IBM standardized the 8-bit byte for the legendary System/360 mainframe, and the 8-bit byte became the global foundation of digital computing!

facts.title: The Symbolics.com Domain Was Registered 40 Years Ago
facts.hook: What is the oldest registered dot-com domain name in the world?
facts.script: On March 15, 1985, Symbolics.com was registered by the Symbolics Computer Corporation, creators of Lisp programming workstations. It was registered four years before the World Wide Web was even invented by Tim Berners-Lee, and remains active online today as a living computing monument!

facts.title: Why CPUs Have L1, L2, and L3 Cache Layers
facts.hook: Why does your processor need three different layers of memory cache inside the chip?
facts.script: Accessing RAM takes about 60 nanoseconds—which is an eternity to a 4 GHz CPU! L1 cache sits directly inside each core and responds in under 1 nanosecond! L2 and L3 caches act as high-speed stepping stones, preventing the CPU from stalling while waiting on system memory!

facts.title: The First Computer Worm Caused $10 Million in Damage
facts.hook: What happened when the first internet worm was unleashed in 1988?
facts.script: Cornell graduate student Robert Tappan Morris wrote a 99-line program to gauge the size of the nascent internet. Due to a coding error, it infected machines repeatedly, paralyzing 10% of all computers connected to ARPANET within 24 hours! It led to the creation of the world's first cybersecurity CERT team!

facts.title: Why GPUs Have Thousands of Cores While CPUs Have 8 to 16
facts.hook: Why does an Nvidia graphics card have 10,000 cores while an Intel CPU has only 16?
facts.script: A CPU core is like a master mathematician that can solve any complex, sequential logic problem with low latency. A GPU core is like a kindergarten student who can only do simple math, but with 10,000 students working simultaneously, they can calculate every pixel and neural network matrix multiplication in parallel!

facts.title: Why Optical Fiber Transmits Data Using Total Internal Reflection
facts.hook: How does glass bend light around the world without losing data?
facts.script: Fiber optic cables are thinner than a human hair and made of pure silica glass. Light pulses travel inside the core by striking the glass-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, causing 100% total internal reflection with virtually zero signal leakage across thousands of miles!

facts.title: Why Python's GIL Limits Multi-Threading
facts.hook: What is Python's Global Interpreter Lock, and why is it controversial?
facts.script: In CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock, or GIL, is a mutex that prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecode simultaneously. It makes memory management safe and simple, but prevents Python from using all CPU cores in CPU-heavy multithreaded tasks!

facts.title: Why RAM Loses Data the Moment Power is Cut
facts.hook: Why can't computer RAM retain files like a storage drive?
facts.script: Dynamic RAM stores each bit as an electrical charge on a microscopic capacitor with a single transistor. Because capacitors naturally leak electricity within milliseconds, RAM must be refreshed with electricity thousands of times per second. Cut the power, and the charge vanishes instantly!

facts.title: The First Computer Animated Movie Used 117 Sun Workstations
facts.hook: How much computer hardware rendered the original 1995 Toy Story?
facts.script: Pixar's 1995 Toy Story was the first entirely computer-animated feature film in history. Pixar used a render farm of 117 dual-processor Sun Microsystems computers running 24/7. Each frame took between 45 minutes and 30 hours to compute, totaling 800,000 machine hours!

facts.title: Why DNS is the Phonebook of the Entire Internet
facts.hook: What actually happens when you type google.com into your browser?
facts.script: Computers don't speak English—they communicate using numerical IP addresses like 142.250.190.46. The Domain Name System, or DNS, acts as the world's master distributed phonebook, translating human-friendly names into binary IP addresses in under 20 milliseconds!

facts.title: Why Quantum Computers Threaten Modern RSA Encryption
facts.hook: How could quantum computers break all current internet encryption?
facts.script: Modern RSA encryption relies on the fact that classical supercomputers take billions of years to factorize massive prime numbers. Shor's quantum algorithm can solve prime factorization exponentially faster, prompting governments and tech giants to develop Post-Quantum Cryptography standards today!

facts.title: The First Apple Computer Sold for Exactly $666.66
facts.hook: Why did Steve Wozniak price the Apple I at $666.66 in 1976?
facts.script: When Steve Wozniak built the hand-crafted Apple I computer, the wholesale cost was about $500. He marked it up by one-third to $666.66 because he liked repeating digits and thought it looked symmetrical, completely unaware of any numerological superstition!
